young.html: René Descartes was a French thinker who lived about 400 years ago. When he finished school, he felt that much of what he had learned was uncertain: teachers disagreed, and old books contradicted each other. Only mathematics seemed sure. So he asked: could I find a way of thinking that works as surely as arithmetic, for every subject?

He made four rules for himself. (1) Don't accept anything as true unless you clearly know it is. (2) Break a hard problem into small pieces. (3) Start with the easiest pieces and climb step by step to the hard ones. (4) Check everything at the end, so nothing is left out. These are good rules for homework, too!

Descartes used his method on science. One puzzle he solved: why is a rainbow round, and why always in the same place in the sky? He studied how sunlight bends and bounces inside a single raindrop, and found that the brightest light comes out at one special angle, about 42 degrees.

young.name: gb-rainbow
young.cap: Light (the colored line) bends going into the drop, bounces off the back, and bends again coming out. Move the slider to try other rays. The tall bar shows where most of the light comes out.

young.html: Make a rainbow. On a sunny morning or late afternoon, stand with your back to the sun and spray a fine mist from a garden hose. Look about halfway between straight ahead and the ground in front of you. Descartes did the same with a big glass ball full of water, raising and lowering it in the sunlight to find where it glowed red.

full.html: René Descartes (1596–1650) was educated at the Jesuit college of La Flèche, studied law, served for a time with armies in the Netherlands and Germany, and settled in the Dutch Republic in 1628, where he lived for about twenty years. In 1637 he published, without his name, a book in French: the Discourse on the Method of Rightly Conducting One's Reason and of Seeking Truth in the Sciences, followed by three essays showing the method at work: the Optics, the Meteors and the Geometry. He wrote in French, not Latin, so that anyone with good sense could read it.

The Discourse is short and personal: the story of how he came to doubt what he had been taught, the rules he chose, the moral code he lived by meanwhile, the famous "I think, therefore I am" (Part IV), a sketch of his physics and of the heart (Part V), and his hopes for science (Part VI). This rung follows the science side; the Meditations rung covers his philosophy of doubt and certainty in full. Descartes's earlier, unfinished Rules for the Direction of the Mind, also in the set, spells out the method in more detail.

The schools taught a science built on Aristotle, with explanations in terms of forms and qualities. New discoveries (the telescope, Kepler's optics, Harvey's circulation) did not fit it well, and scholars argued without end. Descartes wanted a single, certain method that would let reason rebuild knowledge from secure foundations, the way geometers build long chains of proofs from a few simple starting points.

full.text: The first was never to accept anything for true which I did not clearly know to be such … The second, to divide each of the difficulties under examination into as many parts as possible, and as might be necessary for its adequate solution. The third, to conduct my thoughts in such order that, by commencing with objects the simplest and easiest to know, I might ascend by little and little, and, as it were, step by step, to the knowledge of the more complex … And the last, in every case to make enumerations so complete, and reviews so general, that I might be assured that nothing was omitted.
full.author: René Descartes

full.html: Notice what the rules leave out: they say nothing about authority, tradition or the number of people who agree. And notice their source: they are how a mathematician works. Descartes had found that algebra could solve geometry problems by breaking them into steps (see the rung on his Geometry), and he hoped the same order would work everywhere.

full.text: Idea 2: the rainbow, a test case

full.html: In the Meteors Descartes uses his method on the rainbow. He first noticed that a large glass globe filled with water, held in the sun, shines red when the line from his eye to it makes an angle of about 42° with the direction of the sun's rays (measured from the point straight opposite the sun). Then he divided the problem: one drop, one ray at a time. Using the law of refraction, he calculated the path of many rays entering the drop at different heights. Most rays come out spread over many angles, but near 42° they bunch together. Every drop at that angle from your eye sends you this extra-bright light, and the drops at that angle form a circle around the point opposite the sun. With two reflections inside the drop, the rays bunch near 51°: the fainter second bow.

full.name: gb-rainbow
full.cap: Move the ray up and down the drop. Most of the light leaves at many different angles, but near 42° (the tall bar) the rays crowd together. Switch to violet: it bends more and bunches at a slightly smaller angle, which is why the colors separate.

full.html: The law of refraction: $\sin i = n \sin r$, where $i$ is the angle of the ray outside, $r$ inside, and $n \approx 1.33$ for water. For one reflection inside a drop, a ray leaves at an angle $A = 4r - 2i$ from the point opposite the sun. The largest possible $A$, about $42°$ for red light, is the rainbow.

full.title: One ray through a drop
full.q: A ray of red light ($n = 1.331$) strikes a drop at $i = 60°$. Find $r$ and the leaving angle $A = 4r - 2i$.
full.a: r ≈ 40.6°, and the ray leaves at about 42.4°, right in the bow.

full.html: In Part V Descartes describes the body as a kind of machine and gives an account of the heart. He was one of the first well-known writers to accept Harvey's circulation, only nine years after Harvey's book.

full.text: … I need only mention in reply what has been written by a physician of England, who has the honour of having broken the ice on this subject, and of having been the first to teach that there are many small passages at the extremities of the arteries, through which the blood received by them from the heart passes into the small branches of the veins, whence it again returns to the heart; so that its course amounts precisely to a perpetual circulation.
full.note: a footnote mark is left out
full.author: René Descartes

full.html: But Descartes disagreed with Harvey about how the heart moves. He thought heat in the heart made drops of blood boil and swell, pushing open the valves, like milk boiling over. Harvey was right: the heart is a muscle that squeezes.

full.text: Idea 4: science for the good of all

… knowing the force and action of fire, water, air, the stars, the heavens, and all the other bodies that surround us, as distinctly as we know the various crafts of our artizans, we might also apply them in the same way to all the uses to which they are adapted, and thus render ourselves the lords and possessors of nature.
full.author: René Descartes

full.html: Descartes adds that the most important use would be health, the preservation of which is "the first and fundamental" blessing of life. He also asks for public help with experiments, which one person cannot afford alone, much as Bacon did.

items: Why he held back his physics. In Part VI Descartes says he was about to publish a treatise when he learned that "persons to whom I greatly defer" had condemned a doctrine in physics published by another. He meant the Roman Inquisition's condemnation of Galileo in 1633. Descartes's own book, The World, which made the Earth move, was published only after his death.

The law of refraction was not first his. Descartes published the sine law in the Optics. Willebrord Snell had found it about 1621 without publishing, and the Persian mathematician Ibn Sahl had described an equivalent rule around AD 984. English speakers call it Snell's law; in France it is often called Descartes's law.

The rainbow was not first his either, but the numbers were. Theodoric of Freiberg (around 1304) and Kamal al-Din al-Farisi had already traced light through a single drop with water-filled globes. Descartes was the first to calculate the 42° angle from the law of refraction. Why the colors separate had to wait for Newton's prism experiments.

full.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

full.html: Kept: the habit of breaking problems into parts and building up from the simplest; the use of mathematics in physics; the law of refraction; the rainbow angle; the dream of science serving health. Changed: Descartes hoped pure reasoning from clear ideas could reach the laws of nature, with experiments to settle details. Later science, after Newton, leaned much harder on experiment. Descartes's physics of whirlpools (vortices) in a space-filling matter was replaced by Newton's gravity, and his heat theory of the heartbeat by Harvey's muscle pump.

deep.html: Method or methods? Bacon told scientists to gather many cases first; Descartes told them to start from what is certain and reason down. Galileo moved between mathematics and experiment. Most scientists today would say real discovery uses all three. Which of Descartes's four rules do you think matters most?

"Lords and possessors of nature." Descartes, like Bacon, hoped that science would bring health and comfort. Later writers have debated whether this way of speaking about nature encourages care or carelessness. People hold different views; you can weigh them yourself.

How later books answered. Newton's Principia (1687) was partly written against Descartes's physics, and its title, Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy, echoes Descartes's Principles of Philosophy (1644). Newton's Optics (1704) finished the rainbow by explaining its colors.
Big questions. Can any method guarantee the truth? Is it ever wise to doubt everything at once? What do we owe to the people who taught us, if we decide they were wrong?

questions: Try Descartes's four rules on a hard chore or puzzle at home. Which rule helped most?
Descartes wrote in French, not Latin, so ordinary people could read him. Why might that matter?
Descartes held back his own physics after Galileo was condemned. What would you have done?
Descartes accepted Harvey's circulation but got the heartbeat wrong. Is it common to be half right? How do we find the wrong half?
Why is a rainbow always opposite the sun? Could two people standing apart see the same rainbow?
